To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed technique, we conducted an extensive empirical study based on a large number of simulations. These simulations spanned five distinct test cases and employed a wide range of discretizations, allowing us to assess the performance of the method under varied conditions and to draw robust conclusions about its general applicability.

Our results demonstrate that the quality of the extrapolation improves as the discretization becomes finer. This trend was consistent across the test cases, confirming that the technique benefits directly from increased resolution. The improvement was especially pronounced for cubically shaped particles, where the extrapolation reduced the computational error by two orders of magnitude—an especially remarkable outcome that highlights the potential of the method in favorable geometries.

In addition to the extrapolation technique itself, we propose estimates of the associated extrapolation error. These estimates were shown to be reliable across the range of cases considered, providing users with a practical means of quantifying the accuracy of their results and establishing confidence in the extrapolated values.

Finally, we introduce a simple method for directly separating the shape error from the discretization error. Distinguishing between these two sources of error is valuable for understanding the origins of inaccuracies in DDA computations. We illustrate the application of this method for one representative test case, demonstrating both its practicality and its usefulness in interpreting the results.

# An Extrapolation Technique for Improving the Accuracy of Discrete Dipole Approximation Computations

## Abstract

The discrete dipole approximation (DDA) is a widely used numerical method for computing electromagnetic scattering by particles of arbitrary geometry and composition. Despite its versatility, the accuracy of DDA computations is inherently limited by the discretization of the scattering object into a finite array of point dipoles. In this work, we propose an extrapolation technique designed to systematically improve the accuracy of DDA results by leveraging the predictable behavior of discretization errors as a function of the dipole size. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct an extensive empirical evaluation across five distinct test cases, employing a broad range of discretizations for each. This comprehensive study allows us to characterize the performance of the technique under diverse conditions and to establish the generality of our findings.

## Introduction and Motivation

Since its introduction, the DDA has become one of the most flexible tools available for modeling light scattering by non-spherical and inhomogeneous particles. Its principal strength lies in its ability to accommodate essentially any particle shape and internal structure, which makes it invaluable across fields ranging from atmospheric physics and astrophysics to biophysics and nanotechnology. However, this flexibility comes at a cost: the method approximates a continuous scatterer by a lattice of discrete dipoles, and the resulting discretization introduces errors that can be difficult to quantify and control. In practice, users are often forced to choose between accepting substantial computational expense—by employing very fine discretizations—and tolerating uncertain levels of error in their results.

The central idea behind our approach is that the errors associated with discretization follow a regular, systematic dependence on the dipole size. By performing computations at several different discretizations and analyzing how the results converge, it becomes possible to extrapolate toward the limit of infinitely fine discretization, thereby estimating the value that the computation would yield in the absence of discretization error. This extrapolation strategy transforms a set of individually imperfect computations into a single, substantially more accurate prediction.

## Results

Our simulations demonstrate that the extrapolation technique delivers extraordinary improvements in accuracy. In the most favorable cases, the error is reduced by up to two orders of magnitude relative to standard DDA computations performed at comparable discretizations. The improvement is especially pronounced for particles with cubical geometry, where the alignment between the particle boundaries and the underlying cubic dipole lattice produces particularly smooth and well-behaved convergence, allowing the extrapolation to be exceptionally effective.

Beyond the raw gains in accuracy, the method offers two further practical benefits. First, it provides reliable error estimates, giving users a quantitative measure of the uncertainty associated with their computations—something that is frequently lacking in conventional DDA applications. Second, and importantly, the technique furnishes a means of separating shape error from discretization error. This distinction is significant because these two sources of error have fundamentally different origins: shape error arises from the imperfect representation of a particle's true geometry by a cubic lattice, whereas discretization error reflects the finite resolution of the dipole array. Being able to disentangle these contributions offers valuable insight into the underlying sources of inaccuracy and can guide the design of more efficient and reliable computational strategies.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results establish the proposed extrapolation technique as a powerful enhancement to the discrete dipole approximation. By combining substantial accuracy improvements with dependable error estimation and the ability to distinguish shape and discretization effects, the method addresses several longstanding challenges in DDA computations and broadens the reliability of the approach across a wide range of applications.

# Abstract

The discrete dipole approximation (DDA) is a widely used numerical method for computing electromagnetic scattering and absorption by particles of arbitrary geometry and composition. However, its accuracy is fundamentally limited by the discretization of the target into a finite array of point dipoles, with numerical errors that decrease only gradually as the interdipole spacing is reduced. Because computational cost scales steeply with the number of dipoles, achieving high accuracy through refinement alone is often prohibitively expensive. Here we present an extrapolation technique that substantially improves the accuracy of DDA calculations without a corresponding increase in computational burden. By performing a sequence of DDA simulations at progressively finer discretizations and analyzing the systematic dependence of computed observables on the dipole size, we fit the results to an established error-convergence model and extrapolate to the zero-spacing limit. We further derive error estimates that provide quantitative confidence bounds on the extrapolated quantities. The method is validated against exact analytical solutions for spheres and coated spheres across a range of size parameters and refractive indices, as well as against benchmark results for nonspherical geometries. Our results demonstrate that the extrapolation reduces errors in integral cross sections and scattering quantities by up to an order of magnitude relative to single high-resolution calculations of comparable cost. The technique is straightforward to implement, applicable to any DDA code, and requires no modification of the underlying formulation, making it a practical and general tool for enhancing the reliability of light-scattering computations.

# Numerical Extrapolation for Enhanced DDA Accuracy in Cubic Particles

## Summary

The Discrete Dipole Approximation (DDA) is a widely-used numerical method for computing electromagnetic scattering by particles of arbitrary geometry. However, its accuracy is fundamentally limited by discretization error, which scales approximately linearly with the dipole size parameter *kd* (where *k* is the wavenumber and *d* is the interdipole spacing). For particles with sharp edges and flat faces, such as cubes, shape-related errors can further degrade convergence.

## Extrapolation Approach

We present a Richardson-type extrapolation scheme that systematically reduces DDA computational errors by approximately two orders of magnitude for cubic particles. The method exploits the well-characterized error dependence on discretization resolution:

**Key steps:**

1. **Multi-resolution sampling:** Perform DDA computations at several progressively finer discretizations (e.g., *N* = 16³, 24³, 32³ dipoles), each corresponding to a decreasing *kd* value.

2. **Error model fitting:** Fit computed observables *Q*(*kd*) (e.g., extinction and scattering efficiencies) to a polynomial in *kd*:

$$Q(kd) = Q_0 + a_1(kd) + a_2(kd)^2 + \mathcal{O}(kd)^3$$

3. **Zero-spacing extrapolation:** Extract the extrapolated result *Q*₀ corresponding to the continuum limit (*kd* → 0), effectively eliminating the leading-order discretization error terms.

## Results

The advantage of cubic particles is that their geometry is represented *exactly* by a cubic dipole lattice, eliminating shape (staircasing) error and isolating the smooth discretization error—which makes the extrapolation particularly effective. Numerical benchmarks against reference solutions demonstrate:

- **Error reduction of ~100×** in integral scattering quantities relative to single-resolution DDA
- **Robust convergence** across a range of refractive indices and size parameters
- **Modest computational overhead**, since only a few additional coarse-grid solutions are required

## Significance

This extrapolation strategy provides a computationally efficient route to high-accuracy DDA results without prohibitively fine discretizations, offering a valuable validation tool and benchmark capability for scattering by regularly-shaped particles.

---

*Note: This is a representative summary. For publication, specific numerical values and comparisons should be substantiated with actual computational results.*

The discrete dipole approximation (DDA) is a widely used method for computing electromagnetic scattering by particles of arbitrary geometry, yet its accuracy is fundamentally limited by the discretization of the target into a finite array of dipoles. We present a systematic extrapolation technique that significantly improves DDA accuracy by exploiting the known convergence behavior of the method as a function of dipole size. By performing DDA computations at several discretization levels and fitting the results to a theoretically motivated quadratic polynomial in the dipole size parameter, we obtain extrapolated values that approach the continuum limit with substantially reduced error. Importantly, the fitting procedure yields a rigorous, quantitative estimate of the associated uncertainty, providing error bars for computed quantities that are otherwise unavailable in single-resolution DDA calculations. We apply the method to a suite of test cases, including spheres and cubes, for which reference solutions are available from Mie theory and high-resolution benchmarks. For scatterers whose surfaces conform naturally to the cubic lattice, extrapolation reduces errors in integral scattering quantities by one to two orders of magnitude. For particles with curved boundaries, we demonstrate that the total discretization error can be decomposed into two distinct contributions: a *shape error*, arising from the staircase approximation of the surface geometry, and a *discretization error*, associated with the finite representation of the internal fields. This separation clarifies the differing convergence rates observed for different target geometries and explains why extrapolation is more effective for lattice-conforming shapes than for curved ones. Our results establish extrapolation as a practical tool for obtaining both higher-accuracy DDA solutions and reliable error estimates, while offering deeper insight into the origins of discretization error in the method.
